title: Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A.
lead: Akos Swierkiewicz alleged that a younger French colleague displaced him at a French-controlled reinsurer and that he was eventually fired. The lower courts demanded allegations establishing a full prima facie discrimination case; the Supreme Court distinguished that proof framework from what a complaint had to say.

actors.name: Akos Swierkiewicz
actors.role: Hungarian-born former senior vice president and chief underwriting officer alleging discrimination.

actors.name: Sorema N.A.
actors.role: New York reinsurance employer principally owned and controlled by a French parent.

actors.name: François Chavel
actors.role: Sorema’s French chief executive who allegedly demoted and dismissed Swierkiewicz.

actors.name: Nicholas Papadopoulo
actors.role: Younger French employee assigned underwriting responsibilities.

actors.name: Justice Thomas
actors.role: Author of the unanimous Supreme Court opinion.

proceedings: The Southern District of New York dismissed for inadequate discrimination allegations, and the Second Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court reversed and remanded because the complaint met Rule 8 without pleading every element of the evidentiary prima facie case.
limits: The employment events were allegations accepted on review of dismissal. The Court decided pleading sufficiency, not discrimination liability or damages. Its Conley language, rule numbering, and official-form discussion belong to the 2002 procedural setting and do not alone state every current pleading requirement.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A senior insurance employee alleges displacement by a younger colleague
paragraphs: Akos Swierkiewicz, a Hungarian native who was fifty-three when he filed his complaint, joined Sorema N.A. in April 1989 as senior vice president and chief underwriting officer. Sorema was a New York reinsurer principally owned and controlled by a French parent.

Nearly six years later, chief executive François Chavel allegedly demoted Swierkiewicz to marketing and services and assigned most underwriting duties to Nicholas Papadopoulo, a thirty-two-year-old French national like Chavel. About a year after that, Chavel said he wanted to energize the department and appointed Papadopoulo chief underwriting officer. Swierkiewicz alleged that Papadopoulo had one year of underwriting experience compared with his own twenty-six years in insurance.

Swierkiewicz described increasing isolation, exclusion from decisions and meetings, and unsuccessful efforts to discuss his position. In April 1997, he sent Chavel a memorandum explaining his grievances and asking for severance. Two weeks later, company counsel offered resignation without severance or dismissal. When Swierkiewicz refused to resign, Chavel fired him.

sections.title: The complaint is dismissed under a prima facie pleading requirement
sections.cue: What did the lower courts demand?
paragraphs: Swierkiewicz sued for national-origin discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and age discrimination under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA). His account remained allegations, assumed true for reviewing dismissal rather than established findings.

The Southern District of New York dismissed because he had not adequately pleaded circumstances supporting an inference of discrimination. The Second Circuit affirmed under precedent requiring allegations establishing protected-group membership, qualification for the job, an adverse employment action, and circumstances suggesting discrimination. The Supreme Court granted review to resolve a conflict among the circuits over that requirement.

sections.title: An evidentiary framework does not become a pleading checklist
sections.cue: Why did the Court reject importing McDonnell Douglas?
paragraphs: Justice Thomas wrote for a unanimous Court. McDonnell Douglas was the earlier decision organizing the order and allocation of proof in discrimination litigation. Its prima facie showing created an evidentiary inference; the Court had not made every component a prerequisite to pleading. At this stage the question was whether Swierkiewicz could offer evidence supporting his claim, not whether he would ultimately win.

Direct evidence could establish discrimination without every element of that framework, and a plaintiff might find such evidence only in discovery. Requiring more at pleading than might be necessary at trial would be incongruous. In addition, the prima facie formulation was flexible and context-dependent. Before discovery, the appropriate version might not even be clear.

sections.title: The ordinary rules provide notice and tools to test unsupported claims
sections.cue: Why was this particular complaint sufficient?
paragraphs: The Court applied Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a)(2), requiring a short and plain statement, together with Conley’s then-used fair-notice formulation. Discovery could clarify disputed issues, and summary judgment could dispose of unsupported claims. Rule 9(b) specified fraud and mistake for heightened particularity; employment discrimination and municipal liability under §1983 were not listed. The Court would not add another exception judicially. Its discussion of the then-existing official negligence form and former Rules 8(e)(1), 8(f), and 84 illustrated that historical pleading system.

Swierkiewicz identified the protected grounds for his claimed termination and supplied the events, relevant dates, and comparative ages and nationalities. The complaint gave Sorema notice of the claims and their grounds and described relief available under Title VII and the ADEA. The Court did not say an unexplained accusation must always suffice. Rule 12(e) allowed a more definite statement where needed, and Rule 56 addressed claims lacking merit.

sections.title: Policy objections do not authorize a judicially created higher threshold
sections.cue: What did the reversal leave for further proceedings?
paragraphs: Sorema argued that conclusory discrimination claims would burden courts and encourage unsupported suits. The Court answered that the rules contained no special heightened requirement for these claims. A new particularity rule had to come through the rule-amendment process. The sufficiency of a complaint remained distinct from the probability of recovery.

On February 26, 2002, the Supreme Court reversed the Second Circuit and remanded. No separate opinion was issued. Swierkiewicz could proceed beyond the rejected pleading barrier, but the Court did not find discrimination, award damages, or decide the ultimate factual merits. Later pleading decisions, including Twombly, were separate developments.
